routes.description: Establish that early Christian testimony is sufficiently close to apostolic witnesses and historically trustworthy, then use the reported encounters and witness conduct to reduce the plausibility of legend, sincere mistake, and deliberate fabrication in favor of resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the documentary sources warrant an early apostolic resurrection claim, the cumulative evidence materially disfavors the principal non-resurrection explanations, and the resulting comparative inference meets the motion's strong-evidence threshold despite the event's low prior probability.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative historical case makes Jesus's resurrection sufficiently better supported than the live alternatives to constitute strong historical evidence.

centralBridges.description: Establish the proximity, attribution, informed access, independence, and general trustworthiness needed for Pauline, Lukan, Johannine, and related testimony to carry historical weight.
Trace resurrection proclamation and encounter reports to the original apostles early enough to constrain a later-legend explanation.
Show that the character of the reported encounters and witness conduct reduces sincere-mistake and deliberate-fabrication explanations, shifting support toward resurrection.
Explain how multiple convergent evidential lines can overcome a low prior probability without treating unusual content alone as disqualifying.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use independently checkable details, undesigned coincidences, and contextual or literary features as defeasible support for source reliability.
Provide case-specific criteria that distinguish the Christian reports from competing religious or extraordinary claims under a consistent evidential method.

routes.description: Establish that the surviving Christian reports are too anonymous, indirect, dependent, textually uncertain, and inaccessible to investigation to support the claimed resurrection, while preserving ordinary error, story development, and deception as live possibilities.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources lack adequate independent warrant or testability, the move from reports to bodily resurrection remains underdetermined, or the proposed standard cannot distinguish this claim from comparable rejected claims, leaving the strong-evidence threshold unmet.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving reports do not establish resurrection with the strength, testability, and causal connection required by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that anonymity, hearsay, uncertain transmission, dependence, and unavailable examination prevent the reports from functioning like well-grounded eyewitness evidence.
Distinguish the existence or abundance of testimonial claims from independent evidence sufficient to establish the extraordinary event those claims describe.
Preserve legend, shared tradition, sincere error, fabrication, and mixed ordinary explanations without assuming that every narrated encounter occurred as reported.
Require an evidential connection strong enough to overcome the absence of verified comparable resurrections without imposing an a priori prohibition on supernatural events.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether the proposed historical method can accept the Christian reports while principledly rejecting comparable supernatural and religious testimony.
Challenge subsidiary reliability inferences from mundane narrative agreement, vivid detail, embarrassment, martyrdom, and asserted external corroboration.

sections.title: Source Proximity, Attribution, and Testability
sections.rationale: The motion depends first on whether Paul, Acts, the Gospels, and their reported witnesses are sufficiently identifiable, proximate, preserved, and open to verification to ground a strong historical inference.

sections.title: Corroboration, Independence, and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: Claims of undesigned coincidence, ordinary factual accuracy, informed access, and external confirmation must be weighed against shared tradition, literary dependence, textual variation, and the limits of extrapolating from mundane accuracy.

sections.title: Reported Encounters and Competing Explanations
sections.rationale: The central comparative inference turns on whether early proclamation, group and multisensory encounter reports, and witness conduct adequately constrain legend, sincere mistake, deliberate fabrication, or combinations of ordinary causes.

sections.title: Testimonial Standards and Comparative Consistency
sections.rationale: The parties dispute when a claim constitutes evidence, what independent credibility support is required, and whether the same method discriminates consistently among Christian, other religious, and extraordinary reports.

sections.title: Prior Probability, Explanatory Power, and Strong-Evidence Threshold
sections.rationale: Resolution requires connecting the cumulative case or its remaining uncertainties to the motion's demand for strong evidence, including whether low prior probability can be overcome and whether resurrection supplies explanatory power.

routes.description: Establish that secular life and durable social order rely on inherited or extra-natural commitments concerning agency, moral obligation, rational intelligibility, and common purpose that materialist atheism cannot independently ground or institutionally sustain.
routes.successCriteria: The pro burden is satisfied if the identified commitments are necessary for ordinary agency and stable institutions, cannot be adequately derived from materialist premises alone, and are shown to receive distinctive grounding and reinforcement from religious tradition.

motionBridge.description: Connect the indispensable commitments of functional secular life to religious inheritance or extra-natural foundations that ideologically pure atheism cannot supply.

centralBridges.description: Show that meaningful responsibility requires a unified deciding self beyond reductive determinism and that social motivation depends on treating choices as morally consequential.
Show that durable equal law and restraints on self-interest require authoritative moral principles whose force exceeds preference, tribal advantage, or coercion.
Show that religious traditions and God-centered institutions uniquely transmit shared norms, universal identity, family formation, solidarity, and daily support across generations.
Show that religious assumptions about an intelligible universe and reasoned interpretive traditions can support scientific inquiry and moral development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for successful secular conduct by identifying continuing dependence on inherited religious culture, memory, norms, and institutions.
Reconcile morally troubling scripture with objective religious morality through historical accommodation, interpretive development, and universalizing principles.

routes.description: Establish that secular life can acknowledge determinism, construct revisable moral and social arrangements, and pursue truth without professing religious claims whose explanatory, historical, or moral authority remains unsupported.
routes.successCriteria: The con burden is satisfied if secular accounts can explain agency and cooperation without extra-natural premises, religious additions fail to resolve the cited problems, and social utility does not justify belief or instruction that a convinced atheist considers false.

motionBridge.description: Connect secular explanations and critiques to the conclusion that truthful godless life need not depend on religious belief or extra-natural scaffolding.

centralBridges.description: Show that the determined-or-random dilemma applies even to souls, that determinism permits motivated action, and that invoking God does not make libertarian agency intelligible.
Show that human moral arrangements can remain open to correction while alleged divine authority risks insulating mistaken or harmful commands from challenge.
Separate religion's possible social usefulness from its truth and explain why usefulness cannot produce sincere conviction or justify transmitting claims believed false.
Challenge claims of religious dependence by testing whether scientific and moral advances arose through religion, despite it, or through resistance to its authoritative doctrines.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain persistent agency-talk and purposeful behavior as evolutionarily useful features compatible with disbelief in libertarian free will.
Use specific scriptural permissions and feasible omitted reforms to test claims of timeless moral authority and necessary historical accommodation.

sections.title: Free Will, Agency, and Social Responsibility
sections.rationale: The dispute over whether materialism can accommodate a deciding self, whether theism improves the explanation, and whether society needs belief in responsible choice directly tests the alleged extra-natural dependence of secular life.

sections.title: Moral Authority, Equal Law, and Revisability
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of binding moral principles, self-interest, institutional trust, and the correction of harmful norms form a central clash over whether social order requires divine authority.

sections.title: Religion, Science, and Rational Inquiry
sections.rationale: The historical and conceptual relationship between religious assumptions, scientific intelligibility, inherited belief, and institutional resistance bears on whether secular reason borrows its foundations from religion.

sections.title: Scripture, Slavery, and Moral Development
sections.rationale: The exchange over scriptural permissions, historical accommodation, gradual reform, and abolition tests the coherence and practical reliability of claims to transcendent religious morality.

sections.title: Social Cohesion, Cultural Inheritance, and Truth
sections.rationale: Claims about religious institutions, inherited norms, family and communal life, secular alternatives, and the inability to choose belief connect social utility to the motion's ultimate question of truthful secular independence.

moves.speaker: Ben Shapiro
moves.proposition: A functional society needs widespread belief in meaningful agency because people behave and improve more effectively when they believe their choices matter.
moves.attributionBasis: Shapiro resumes from the nihilism issue, explicitly connects it to religion's social good, and sustains the argument until O'Connor answers the evolutionary-illusion point.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Any mental event is either determined by prior causes or undetermined and random, so neither a material mind nor an immaterial soul makes libertarian free will intelligible.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor first accepts that evolution supplies an experienced illusion of purpose, then presents a continuous excluded-middle argument before Shapiro directly challenges it.

moves.speaker: Ben Shapiro
moves.proposition: If people believe in a deciding self, materialism cannot accommodate that belief, while functional society nevertheless requires widespread belief in morally weighty choice.
moves.attributionBasis: Shapiro explicitly restates his original claim as conditional, concedes that free will might be false, and then returns uninterrupted to the social necessity argument.

components.text: Why a deciding self escapes the exhaustive choice between prior determination and undetermined randomness.

response.rationale: The reply returns to the social need for morally weighty choice and asserts materialism cannot accommodate a deciding self, but it does not identify a flaw in the determined-or-random dilemma.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it is closely issue-bearing and clarifies the pro conditional, yet leaves the dilemma's decisive inference uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional form is explicit, but deciding self, materialism, and functional society retain material ambiguity and broad population scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Conceding that free will might be false appropriately qualifies the metaphysical claim, but the asserted societal necessity remains much stronger than the supplied warrant.

charity.alternative: Determinists can regard deliberation as causally effective and morally important without believing in libertarian self-origination.
charity.decisiveQualification: The claim needs to distinguish meaningful determined deliberation from the nihilistic attitude attributed to materialism.

routes.description: Establish classical theism by reasoning from the present dependence, contingency, and actualization of created things to a necessary sustaining source, then defend the coherence and goodness of that source against objections from freedom, temporal knowledge, evil, and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if vertical causal dependence requires a necessary and purely actual divine ground, the relevant divine attributes remain mutually coherent, and suffering, nonbelief, and religious diversity are compatible with providential goodness and revelation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the necessary explanatory source reached through Thomistic metaphysics possesses the attributes required for the God of classical theism and remains credible after the principal objections.

centralBridges.description: Establish that contingent beings and act-potency causal series require a concurrent sustaining cause rather than merely an earliest temporal cause.
Connect the sustaining explanatory source to pure actuality and the divine attributes characteristic of classical theism.
Explain how pure actuality permits divine freedom and how eternal causal knowledge encompasses temporal change without change in God.
Reconcile divine goodness and providence with creaturely evil, suffering, hiddenness, and diverse forms of religious access.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why knowledge of God can be naturally accessible while remaining difficult enough to warrant revelation and unequal human uptake.
Supply the teleological and analogical framework needed to predicate goodness of God and evaluate created suffering within an ordered whole.

routes.description: Undermine classical theism by challenging the inferences from dependent causal series to one purely actual, good, worship-worthy God and by arguing that pure actuality conflicts with divine freedom and changing knowledge while evolutionary suffering and nonresistant nonbelief count against perfect providential love.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the Thomistic causal arguments leave material explanatory or identification gaps, classical divine attributes generate unresolved contradictions, or the observed patterns of suffering and nonbelief are sufficiently unexpected under a perfectly good and loving God.

motionBridge.description: Show that the proposed classical God is not established by the Thomistic arguments and is independently undermined by conceptual and evidential objections.

centralBridges.description: Challenge concurrent conservation, termination, common-cause, pure-actuality, perfect-goodness, and worship-worthiness steps in the Thomistic inference.
Argue that a purely actual and immutable God cannot possess alternative-possibility freedom or knowledge responsive to a changing temporal world.
Establish that extensive apparently gratuitous animal suffering is improbable under perfect providential goodness and remains morally assessable.
Argue that nonresistant unbelief and persistent incompatible religious traditions conflict with the expectations generated by perfect divine love.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground objective judgments about needless suffering in irreducible normative truths without requiring natural teleology or a divine creator.
Present existential inertia as a coherent alternative to the claim that creatures require continuous divine conservation.

sections.title: Causal Dependence, Conservation, and Identification of God
sections.rationale: This issue contains the affirmative route from contingent, actualized beings to a sustaining necessary cause and the objections concerning existential inertia, infinite or multiple termini, pure actuality, goodness, and worship-worthiness.

sections.title: Pure Actuality and Divine Freedom
sections.rationale: The compatibility of pure actuality with free creation is a distinct burden because classical theism must explain how divine action is internally principled and genuinely free without unrealized potentialities or alternative possibilities.

sections.title: Immutability, Eternity, and Knowledge of Temporal Change
sections.rationale: This section tests whether eternal causal knowledge can encompass changing temporal truths without acquisition or loss in God, including challenges arising across competing theories of time.

sections.title: Evolutionary Evil, Divine Goodness, and Providence
sections.rationale: The scale and apparent gratuitousness of animal and human suffering directly bear on perfect goodness, while the opposing framework invokes transcendence, privation, creaturely freedom, redemptive goods, teleology, and cosmic order.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Revelation, and Religious Diversity
sections.rationale: This issue joins claims about natural accessibility and accommodated revelation with objections from nonresistant nonbelief and religious disagreement, testing what epistemic access a perfectly loving God would provide.

routes.description: Establish that Paul understood Jesus as an earthly historical person by combining Pauline biographical and familial references with an earthly reading of the crucifying rulers and corroboration from sources connected to Paul and the Gospel tradition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the Pauline references are best explained as ordinary historical claims, the rulers passage situates the crucifixion among human authorities, and the proposed Acts and Gospel corroboration remains sufficiently independent and reliable to reinforce that reading.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative evidence is better explained by Paul referring to a human Jesus who lived and was crucified on Earth than by a wholly celestial setting for the saving events.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline references to ancestry, birth, teachings, associates, betrayal, and execution supply meaningful historical particularity.
Establish from the context of First Corinthians that the rulers responsible for the crucifixion are human authorities, even if spiritual forces also participated.
Show that references to James and other brothers of the Lord are most coherently understood as biological relationships to Jesus.
Establish that Acts is substantially reliable and connected to a companion of Paul, making its historical Jesus relevant to reconstructing Paul's understanding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a sufficiently broad Pauline corpus so that relevant historical references are not excluded solely by disputed authorship judgments.
Show that dispersed incidental correspondences among Gospel narratives are more expected on historical information than deliberate literary harmonization.

routes.description: Establish that Paul's accepted letters do not securely locate Jesus's ministry, death, and resurrection on Earth, while their cosmic language permits a flesh-bearing celestial figure killed by demonic rulers in a mythic heavenly realm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline biographical and familial expressions remain materially ambiguous, the rulers and cosmology make a heavenly crucifixion viable, and Acts and Gospel narratives cannot independently import a later earthly biography into Paul's letters.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest relevant Pauline evidence remains compatible with, and materially supports, a mortal embodied Jesus whose death and resurrection occurred in a celestial rather than terrestrial realm.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the accepted Pauline letters lack an unambiguous earthly ministry or terrestrial location for Jesus's death and resurrection.
Show that the rulers of the age can be celestial demonic powers and that their concealed knowledge and interests fit that interpretation.
Establish that ancient cosmology allowed heavenly counterparts of earthly places, objects, and practices, making a celestial crucifixion intelligible.
Show that Acts and the Gospels are too disputed, literary, dependent, or historically unstable to determine what Paul believed about Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Pauline brother-of-the-Lord language can identify an ordinary baptized Christian rather than a biological sibling of Jesus.
Supply the comparative possibility that a savior cult could later place a nonhistorical divine figure into an earthly narrative.

sections.title: Pauline Biography, Silence, and Corpus Scope
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether the relevant Pauline letters contain historical markers sufficient to locate Jesus on Earth, and whether the admissible Pauline corpus expands or restricts that evidence.

sections.title: The Rulers and the Realm of Crucifixion
sections.rationale: The identity of the rulers of the age and the cosmological intelligibility of heavenly counterparts directly distinguish an earthly execution by human authorities from a celestial passion involving demonic powers.

sections.title: James and the Brothers of the Lord
sections.rationale: Whether Paul's references identify biological relatives or members of a baptized cultic family is among the most direct disputes over historical particularity within the Pauline evidence.

sections.title: Acts, Pauline Chronology, and Companion Authorship
sections.rationale: Acts can connect Paul to a thoroughly historical Jesus only if its chronology, factual reliability, first-person narration, and claimed relationship to a Pauline companion survive the competing literary explanation.

sections.title: Gospel Independence and Undesigned Coincidences
sections.rationale: The evidential value of cross-Gospel correspondences depends on whether dispersed details reflect independent historical information or deliberate adaptation and harmonization of earlier narrative sources.

routes.description: Establish that current research findings remain too remote from a materially adequate account of life's emergence and that broader representations of those findings convey substantially greater explanatory proximity than the evidence supports.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the remaining transition from simple chemistry to organized, heritable, evolving cellular systems is shown to be unresolved under meaningful empirical criteria, while current research claims or narratives are shown to obscure or exceed that limitation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved chemistry-to-life gap to a substantial mismatch between demonstrated progress and communicated explanatory proximity.

centralBridges.description: Require an account of how simple chemistry becomes materially organized, information-bearing, heritable, and evolvable biological machinery.
Require discriminating empirical standards for metabolism, replication, fidelity, heredity, and life rather than reliance on broadly lifelike behavior.
Show that limited chemical results or early organizing principles do not by themselves warrant claims of substantial proximity to cellular life.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish criticism of present evidentiary adequacy from a claim that a future naturalistic explanation is impossible.
Ground the critique in naturalistic evidentiary requirements rather than a design inference or theological objection.

routes.description: Establish that substantial explanatory progress need not reproduce Earth's exact history or begin with modern cells because experiments and theory can identify testable generative principles linking simple chemistry, information, selection, and evolving organization.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if measurable chemical organization and selection provide a falsifiable staged pathway toward biological functionality, and if present claims are appropriately limited to emerging mechanisms rather than completion of a full historical or cellular account.

motionBridge.description: Connect reproducible, falsifiable steps from chemistry toward evolving organization to a warranted claim that an explanatory pathway is emerging.

centralBridges.description: Identify simple natural principles capable of generating molecular complexity, templating, coupled catalysis, or primitive copying.
Explain how heritable chemical variation and selection can develop increasingly functional organization toward biological systems.
Provide objective measurements and experimental predictions that can distinguish progress from unconstrained historical speculation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate evidence for a general pathway from claims to know the unique molecular sequence followed on early Earth.
Require uncertainty, experimental revision, and collaborative scrutiny to constrain ambitious origin-of-life hypotheses.

sections.title: Scope of Present Claims and the Standard for Overstatement
sections.rationale: This issue determines what current research is claiming, whether an emerging pathway is distinct from a completed explanation, and whether public or scientific extrapolation materially exceeds the demonstrated results.

sections.title: The Explanatory Gap from Simple Chemistry to Cellular Life
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether the distance between simple chemical environments and organized cellular systems is an unresolved burden-defining gap or a bridgeable sequence whose governing principles are becoming accessible.

sections.title: What Laboratory Chemical Systems Demonstrate
sections.rationale: The relevance of templating, autocatalysis, coupled catalytic organization, and primitive copying determines whether laboratory results disclose mechanisms continuous with life or remain isolated chemical achievements.

sections.title: Operational Definitions and Objective Measures of Life-like Progress
sections.rationale: Standards for information, metabolism, replication, fidelity, complexity, and life establish what observations would count as genuine explanatory progress and keep the dispute empirically testable.

sections.title: Generative Principles, Selection, and Predictive Pathways
sections.rationale: The viability of complexity-based theory, chemical selection, and experimentally testable predictions bears on whether research offers a cumulative natural pathway rather than either a historical narrative or an admission of ignorance.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the better account of reality through a cumulative comparison involving biological information and organization, cosmic features, resurrection testimony, and the compatibility of divine goodness with nonbelief, religious geography, and suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its positive design and resurrection inferences jointly favor Christian theism over naturalism and its explanations of hiddenness and suffering prevent the principal naturalistic counterevidence from reversing that comparison.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined positive evidence and answers to counterevidence make the observed reality more expected under Christian theism than under atheistic naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Connect biological information, genetic-code optimization, and interdependent replication systems to intelligent causation rather than unguided naturalistic origins.
Establish that the testimonial and historical data are better explained by Jesus's resurrection than by deception, mistake, development, hallucination, or other naturalistic alternatives.
Explain sincere nonbelief and uneven religious access consistently with divine love, adequate evidence, moral probation, proportionate judgment, and mercy.
Limit the disconfirming force of human and animal suffering by identifying relevant goods, evidential dependencies, epistemic limits, or features of an orderly world.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend likelihood-based and positive-causal inference as appropriate methods for comparing theism and naturalism without treating every unresolved mechanism as decisive.
Use cosmic beginning, fine-tuning, religious history, or public corroboration as supporting considerations within the cumulative comparison.

routes.description: Establish atheistic naturalism as the better account by challenging design and resurrection inferences, explaining religious belief and experience naturalistically, and treating sincere nonbelief, religious geography, and apparently gratuitous suffering as evidence against Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations or warranted uncertainty undercut the principal positive arguments for Christian theism while hiddenness, culturally patterned religion, and suffering remain more expected under naturalism.

motionBridge.description: Show that naturalistic explanations plus the comparative counterevidence account for the observed reality better than Christian theism does.

centralBridges.description: Show that unresolved biological origins or complexity do not warrant intelligent design and remain appropriately addressed through natural mechanisms, scientific development, or suspended judgment.
Show that textual development, uncertain testimony, neurological or psychological experiences, and ordinary historical explanations remain preferable to a resurrection inference.
Establish that sincere nonbelief and culturally patterned religious distribution are expected under naturalism but conflict with an adequately revealing and perfectly loving God.
Establish that apparently purposeless human and animal suffering is more expected under naturalism and is not adequately explained by stable laws, unknown divine reasons, or human-centered goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require positive comparative support before moving from gaps in current naturalistic knowledge to supernatural or specifically Christian conclusions.
Explain religious belief and consoling narratives through cultural, psychological, or neurological processes that do not presuppose their truth.

sections.rationale: The affirmative's principal design case rests on DNA and RNA information, genetic-code optimization, replication, and irreducible complexity, while the opposing burden is to test whether these support intelligence or merely expose unresolved natural history.

sections.title: Resurrection testimony and naturalistic alternatives
sections.rationale: The resurrection case is the principal route from general theistic possibility to specifically Christian theism, making testimonial reliability, Gospel development, apostolic conduct, prior probability, and alternative experiences central to the motion.

sections.title: Divine hiddenness, sincere nonbelief, and religious geography
sections.rationale: Nonresistant nonbelief and geographically uneven religion directly compare what a loving revelatory God and a culturally mediated naturalistic world would lead observers to expect.

sections.title: Human and animal suffering under theism and naturalism
sections.rationale: Apparently gratuitous, minor, and animal suffering supplies a major comparative challenge to divine goodness, while theistic replies invoke orderly laws, possible goods, evidential dependence, and limits on human access to reasons.

sections.title: Comparative inference, religious experience, and worldview explanation
sections.rationale: The debate repeatedly disputes when likelihoods, scientific track records, causal analogies, supernatural mechanisms, and naturalistic genealogies of religious belief legitimately shift the comparison between the worldviews.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative body of historical facts concerning burial, the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the origin of resurrection belief, then show that bodily resurrection may be considered historically and explains those facts better than competing accounts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the core facts are sufficiently established, the inference to divine bodily resurrection is methodologically admissible, and that hypothesis has greater comparative explanatory adequacy than the relevant naturalistic or rival theological alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus' bodily resurrection is the best explanation of the historically established aftermath of the crucifixion.

centralBridges.description: Establish the burial, empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and emergence of sincere resurrection belief as facts requiring a unified explanation.
Show that historical reasoning may compare a divine-resurrection hypothesis with alternatives without excluding it solely because it invokes supernatural agency.
Demonstrate that resurrection accounts for the relevant facts with stronger explanatory scope, fit, and plausibility than the competing hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the adequacy of early traditions and central narrative agreement despite disputed authorship, transmission, interests, and differences in detail.
Use Jewish bodily-resurrection concepts and Jesus' religious-historical context to distinguish the proposed explanation from visions and ad hoc supernatural alternatives.

routes.description: Challenge the reliability and interpretation of the claimed historical facts, explain the aftermath through historically accessible developments or natural scenarios, and show that historical method cannot privilege divine bodily resurrection as the best explanation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the factual foundation remains materially underdetermined, historically accessible alternatives remain available, or shared historical criteria cannot assign comparative superiority to the proposed divine-resurrection explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical evidence does not establish Jesus' bodily resurrection as the best historical explanation of what followed the crucifixion.

centralBridges.description: Apply historical source criteria to contest the reliability, independence, consistency, and interpretation of the traditions supporting the proposed core facts.
Show that historical inquiry based on shared probabilistic standards cannot establish unobservable divine action as its preferred conclusion.
Provide historically accessible accounts of burial uncertainty, visions, scriptural reinterpretation, belief development, and narrative growth that reduce the need for bodily resurrection.
Show that the evidence cannot uniquely select the proposed Christian divine explanation over natural scenarios or rival theological interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify literary or theological functions that could account for the Joseph and women traditions without treating their awkwardness as decisive authenticity evidence.
Require a consistent evidential standard across resurrection claims and other ancient miracle reports rather than privileging one inherited tradition.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Evidentiary Standards
sections.rationale: The reliability, independence, dating, transmission, consistency, and appropriate use of the documentary traditions determine how much of the proposed factual foundation is available for any later explanatory inference.

sections.title: Burial and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: The identifiable burial and claimed discovery of an empty tomb supply the principal physical-evidence line for bodily resurrection, while disputes over Joseph, the women, invention, and body removal directly test that line.

sections.title: Appearances and the Origin of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: Reported postmortem experiences and the disciples' resulting convictions require interpretation as bodily encounters, visions, developing scriptural beliefs, or some combination, making this a central causal dispute.

sections.title: Miracle Probability and the Scope of History
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether historical inference may admit divine action and whether antecedent improbability, specific evidence, shared assumptions, and explanatory comparison can make resurrection historically preferable.

sections.title: Competing Explanations, Underdetermination, and Context
sections.rationale: Naturalistic scenarios, developmental accounts, rival supernatural stories, and Jesus' religious-historical context determine whether resurrection uniquely integrates the evidence or remains one interpretation among alternatives.

routes.description: Establish Christian revelation as the necessary precondition for intelligible truth, logic, knowledge, induction, and evidence, then argue that skeptical or naturalistic alternatives cannot supply those preconditions without circularity or borrowing them.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if God and Christian revelation are shown to be necessary for the rational practices used in assessing the motion, while the proposed nonrevelatory foundations fail to account for those practices and rival-revelation objections are resolved.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessity of the Christian God for intelligibility to the conclusion that belief in God is reasonable under the debate motion.

centralBridges.description: Require divine revelation to ground objective truth, access to reality, and knowledge despite skeptical possibilities.
Account for logical necessity and rational thought as reflections of God's mind rather than unexplained natural processes.
Show that nonrevelatory appeals to past experience cannot non-circularly justify induction or expectations about the future.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why evidence is assessed within a God-grounded framework rather than from a purportedly neutral standpoint.
Distinguish Christian revelation from competing religious claims and internal Christian disagreement sufficiently to support the specifically Christian foundation.

routes.description: Apply an evidential and fallibilist standard of reasonable belief, defend practical truth-seeking through shared experience, logic, and probabilistic induction, and require independent support for God, supernatural causation, revelation, and Christianity's claimed exclusivity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if reasonable inquiry can proceed without absolute certainty or Christian revelation and if presupposing God does not independently demonstrate divine existence, explanatory necessity, reliable revelation, or warranted belief in the specifically Christian claim.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of a valid, sound, and adequately evidenced demonstration of God to withholding belief under the motion's reasonableness standard.

centralBridges.description: Establish that justified belief and practical inquiry do not require infallible access to ultimate reality or a solution to hard solipsism.
Account for truth-seeking, logical reasoning, and induction through reality, shared experience, and evidence-proportioned confidence.
Require demonstration that Christianity uniquely grounds rational intelligibility rather than treating that exclusivity as a premise or shifting its burden.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether conflicting revelations, scriptural claims, and transmission history provide a reliable method for identifying divine disclosure.
Require a demonstrable method or causal connection before supernatural explanations can support reasonable God-belief.

sections.title: Reasonableness, Burden of Proof, and Presuppositional Method
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the motion-level standard and determines whether God may be treated as the prerequisite of adjudication or must be supported through shared argumentative and evidential standards.

sections.title: Truth, Knowledge, Certainty, and Hard Solipsism
sections.rationale: The central epistemic clash concerns whether knowledge requires divinely guaranteed access to ultimate reality or whether fallible, reality-directed inquiry can support reasonable belief without absolute certainty.

sections.title: Logic, Reason, and Worldview Grounding
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether logical absolutes and rational cognition require the Christian God, and whether naming God as their foundation supplies a demonstrated and uniquely necessary account.

sections.title: Induction, Evidence, and Supernatural Inquiry
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether probabilistic inference from experience is rationally adequate, whether it is problematically circular, and what evidential method could warrant supernatural causation.

sections.title: Revelation, Rival Claims, and Christian Specificity
sections.rationale: Because the affirmative foundation is specifically Christian revelation, the burden structure includes how revelation is identified, how competing religious claims are distinguished, and how internal disagreement bears on reliability.

routes.description: Establish that divine simplicity follows from classical commitments concerning aseity and pure actuality, then explain apparent plurality, Trinitarian relations, freedom, and contingent knowledge without introducing real intrinsic composition or change in God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its account excludes intrinsic parts on principled metaphysical grounds while preserving intelligible divine attributes, real Trinitarian relational distinction, free creation or noncreation, and omniscient knowledge of contingent and changing reality.

motionBridge.description: Show that one intrinsically simple divine reality can satisfy the classical-theist, Trinitarian, freedom, and omniscience commitments named in the motion.

centralBridges.description: Derive the exclusion of intrinsic composition from aseity, explanatory independence, or the pure actuality required of a first cause.
Distinguish real intrinsic composition from grounded conceptual distinctions, analogical predication, and extrinsic creature-directed predications.
Explain how persons and opposed procession-relations can be identical with the divine essence without becoming additional intrinsic constituents.
Explain contingent and temporally varying knowledge attributions through an immutable divine intellect and causal efficacy together with extrinsic truths and creaturely changes.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Treat distinct alleged forms of composition separately while identifying the act-potency principles that connect them.
Account for creation and noncreation as free possibilities that neither complete nor intrinsically improve God.

routes.description: Define the intrinsic distinctions prohibited by simplicity and show that classical theism's positive commitments generate at least one such distinction through dependence, Trinitarian processions, free contingent knowledge, or knowledge of changing reality.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed reconciliations cannot preserve the relevant Trinitarian or epistemic realities without admitting a positive intrinsic distinction, contingent state, potentiality, or change inconsistent with divine simplicity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the commitments named in the motion require distinctions or changes that an intrinsically partless God cannot coherently possess.

centralBridges.description: Specify which positive ontological items or distinctions count as intrinsic constituents and why simplicity excludes them.
Show that divine independence can be understood without eliminating every intrinsic distinction, undermining the inference from aseity to simplicity.
Show that real processions, opposed relations, or asymmetric personal predicates require distinctions not reducible to the undifferentiated divine essence.
Show that free noncreation or changing contingent truths require contingent intrinsic knowledge or epistemic change incompatible with immutability and pure actuality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require an account of what divine knowledge consists in if its contingent differentiation is assigned wholly or principally to extrinsic reality.
Establish the availability of an alone world through divine freedom, self-sufficiency, or reasons compatible with refraining from creation.

sections.title: Metaphysical content, parts, and divine predication
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what simplicity excludes and whether conceptual, analogical, relational, or truthmaker-based distinctions preserve meaningful divine attributes without adding positive intrinsic constituents.

sections.title: Aseity, pure actuality, and the exclusion of composition
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal positive grounds for simplicity and the counterclaim that divine independence can survive intrinsic multiplicity under alternative accounts of dependence, grounding, and unity.

sections.title: Trinitarian persons, processions, and subsistent relations
sections.rationale: This issue directly addresses whether real personal and procession-based distinctions can be identical with one divine essence or instead constitute intrinsic plurality prohibited by simplicity.

sections.title: Divine freedom and knowledge of contingent, changing reality
sections.rationale: This issue joins the creationless-world and changing-truth objections with accounts of extrinsic predication, immutable intellect, causality, and creaturely relations, covering the motion's central freedom and omniscience requirements.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative inference to Christian theism by connecting a finite cosmic past, life-permitting physical conditions, the emergence of life, the character of biblical revelation, and a Christian account of suffering to a purposive creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the scientific considerations are shown to be more expected under purposive creation than under materialism, the biblical material remains credible as revelation, and suffering can be reconciled with the goodness and redemptive purposes attributed to the Christian God.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined scientific, biblical, and moral considerations increase the comparative plausibility of the Christian God.

centralBridges.description: Connect evidence against an eternal past to a cosmic beginning for which a creator is an appropriate explanation.
Show that life-permitting parameters and the origin or complexity of life call for explanation and are expected under purposive agency.
Defend the Bible's theological and cosmological claims as compatible with its ancient genre and indicative of revelation rather than ordinary mythmaking.
Supply a coherent Christian account under which natural suffering and divine actions remain compatible with divine goodness and redemption.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify limits in materialist accounts of mind and the natural world's apparent order that can support the cumulative creator inference.

routes.description: Establish that the cited scientific phenomena do not warrant a creator inference and that biblical cosmology, natural suffering, and scriptural violence are more expected under human religious development than under an omniscient and benevolent Christian God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if cosmological and fine-tuning inferences remain underdetermined, naturalistic alternatives remain viable, biblical claims lack distinctive evidential authority, and suffering supplies independent evidence against the character attributed to the Christian God.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined scientific, biblical, and suffering evidence does not increase, and may reduce, the comparative plausibility of the Christian God.

centralBridges.description: Show that current cosmology and arguments about infinity do not establish an absolute beginning or uniquely support creation.
Challenge fine-tuning and origin-of-life probability claims while preserving scientifically motivated or otherwise non-theistic explanations.
Show that biblical cosmology shares ancient motifs or errors and therefore lacks the distinctiveness expected from divine revelation.
Show that prehuman suffering, natural cruelty, and scriptural violence conflict with divine goodness and resist the proposed redemptive explanations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a physical account of consciousness and include both natural beauty and natural harm when assessing design-based inferences.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Theorems, and an Eternal Past
sections.rationale: Whether cosmology, thermodynamics, physical finitude, and arguments about infinity establish an absolute beginning is a major premise connecting scientific evidence to a creator.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Naturalistic Alternatives, and the Origin of Life
sections.rationale: This section tests whether life-permitting parameters and biological origins favor purposive design or remain underdetermined because probabilities and non-theistic alternatives are unresolved.

sections.title: Biblical Cosmology, Genre, and Revelatory Credibility
sections.rationale: The evidential status of Genesis and other biblical claims bears directly on whether Scripture displays divine insight or the ordinary cosmology and literary forms of ancient cultures.

sections.title: Animal Suffering, Scriptural Violence, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: Prehuman suffering and biblical violence directly test the compatibility of the observed and scriptural worlds with the goodness, justice, and redemptive purposes attributed to the Christian God.

sections.title: Natural Order, Beauty, and Materialist Accounts of Mind
sections.rationale: Arguments from beauty, complexity, and consciousness provide supporting comparative evidence about purposive creation and the explanatory reach of physicalism, while remaining subsidiary to the named principal domains.
